title: Start a fire with a battery and steel wool
mechanism_check: Fire needs heat, fuel, and oxygen in sequence: tinder catches, kindling builds, fuel sustains.
Steel wool shorts the battery terminals, the fine strands glow white-hot — that's your heat.
Prepare ALL fuel stages before striking: tinder bundle, pencil-thick kindling, wrist-thick fuel.
improvised_tools: Fine (0000) steel wool + any battery 3V+ (AA pair, 9V, phone battery).
Dry tinder: char cloth, dryer lint, shredded bark, or a cotton ball with petroleum jelly.
A knife or sharp edge to feather kindling.
steps: Build the fire lay first: tinder bundle in the center, kindling teepee over it, fuel nearby.
Stretch a thin tuft of steel wool between the battery terminals — it ignites in seconds.
Drop the glowing wool into the tinder bundle and blow gently into flame.
Feed kindling progressively; don't smother the young flame with big wood.
stop_conditions: Fire bans or extreme fire danger: stop — no improvised fire is worth a wildfire.
Wind scattering embers toward dry fuel: stop and shelter instead; an escaped fire is a second emergency.

title: Pre-filter murky water with cloth and settling, then purify
mechanism_check: Murky water clogs filters and shields pathogens from chemical treatment — clarity first, kill second.
Settling drops silt by gravity; cloth catches the rest. Neither kills pathogens.
Purification is a separate step: boil or chemical dose after the water runs clear.
improvised_tools: A bandana, shirt, or coffee filter as a pre-filter; two containers for settle-and-pour.
Fire + metal container for boiling; plain unscented bleach as backup.
steps: Let the water sit 30 minutes; pour off the clear top without disturbing the silt.
Pour through folded cloth into a clean container.
Boil rolling for 1 minute (3 at altitude) — or 2 drops bleach per liter, wait 30 minutes.
Store in the cleanest container you have, covered.
stop_conditions: Chemical smell, oily sheen, or unnatural color: stop — no field method removes chemical contamination.
No way to boil or dose: pre-filtered water is still unsafe — keep looking for a better source.

title: Taut-line hitch for adjustable shelter lines
mechanism_check: Guy lines need adjusting as fabric sags and wind shifts — a fixed knot can't do that.
The taut-line hitch grips under load but slides when unloaded: friction wraps do the work.
improvised_tools: Any cordage: paracord, shoelaces, bank line — even torn fabric strips in a pinch.
No tools needed; practice on a tent stake or tree.
steps: Wrap the working end twice around the standing line inside the loop, then once outside.
Dress the wraps snug and parallel — crossed wraps slip.
Slide the hitch to tension the line; it locks when loaded.
Test by pulling the line hard — adjust until it holds.
stop_conditions: Cord too slick or stiff to hold wraps (some synthetics): stop and use a trucker's hitch instead.
Load-bearing climbing or rescue: stop — this is a camp knot, never life-safety rigging.

title: Splint a broken tent pole in the field
mechanism_check: Tent poles fail at the ferrule or mid-section; the shock cord still threads through if the break is clean.
The splint must be rigid and longer than the break, lashed so the pole can't flex at the fracture.
improvised_tools: A tent stake, sturdy stick, or spare pole section as the splint.
Duct tape, athletic tape, or cordage for lashing.
The pole's own shock cord keeps sections aligned while you work.
steps: Straighten the broken sections along the shock cord.
Lay the splint alongside the break, spanning well past it both ways.
Lash tightly with tape or cord at both ends of the splint.
Re-thread and tension the tent; the splinted section takes less load — guy it out well.
stop_conditions: Multiple breaks or a shattered ferrule: the pole is done — reconfigure the tent around the missing pole.
Splint flexing under tent tension: stop and shorten the span or double the splint.

title: Field-repair a torn pack strap
mechanism_check: Straps fail at stitching or buckles; webbing itself rarely tears mid-length.
The repair must hold the same load direction the strap was designed for.
improvised_tools: Duct tape wrapped in a spiral (sticky side out first, then sticky in) for webbing tears.
A safety pin, zip tie, or cord as a buckle substitute; a needle and dental floss for stitching.
steps: For torn webbing: overlap the ends 3 inches and spiral-wrap with duct tape, pulling tight.
For a broken buckle: thread the strap through a carabiner, ring, or tied cord loop.
For pulled stitching: restitch with dental floss in a box-X pattern.
Load-test with body weight before trusting it on the trail.
stop_conditions: Load-bearing climbing or safety gear: stop — field repairs are for packs, never protection.
Webbing UV-rotted along its length: patching one spot just moves the failure.

title: Improvise an emergency whistle and signal mirror
mechanism_check: Sound carries farther than shouting and doesn't exhaust you; light flashes are visible for miles to aircraft.
Three of anything is the distress pattern: three blasts, three flashes.
improvised_tools: A commercial whistle is best; improvise with a blade of grass between thumbs or a hollow reed.
Any mirror, phone screen, or polished metal (even a can lid) for flashing.
steps: Whistle: 3 sharp blasts, pause 1 minute, repeat — keep a sustainable rhythm.
Mirror: catch the sun and sweep the reflection across the horizon and at aircraft sound.
At night: 3 flashes with any light source, repeated.
Stay put while signaling — movement makes you harder to find.
stop_conditions: No whistle and no mirror: use rock-on-rock clacks or bright cloth waving — anything rhythmic and unnatural.
Exhaustion setting in: signal in bursts and rest — steady weak signaling beats a frantic burst then silence.

title: Hang food safe from animals with no carabiners
mechanism_check: Bears and rodents defeat hangs that are too low, too close to the trunk, or on weak branches.
The PCT method: one rope over a branch, bag clipped mid-rope, counterweight — no carabiner needed with knots.
improvised_tools: 50+ feet of cord; a rock in a sock as a throw weight.
A sturdy stuff sack for food; a stick as a toggle instead of a carabiner.
steps: Find a branch 15+ feet up, 6+ feet from the trunk, that holds your weight test.
Throw the weighted line over; tie the food bag to the line with a secure knot.
Hoist until the bag is 10+ feet up and 4+ feet below the branch.
Tie off to the trunk; hang everything scented — food, trash, toiletries.
stop_conditions: Grizzly country with no good branch: stop hanging and use a bear canister or the provided storage.
Branch flexing under your weight test: find another — a dropped bag at night is a bear dinner bell.

title: Choose and prepare an emergency bivvy site
mechanism_check: Site selection is the shelter: high and dry beats any tarp configuration.
Cold ground, wind, and water are the three heat thieves — the site must defeat all three.
improvised_tools: Your eyes first: read drainage, wind, and widow-makers (dead branches overhead).
Dry leaves and duff for a mattress; a trash bag or poncho for a roof.
steps: Pick high ground out of wind, away from dry creek beds and lone trees.
Clear sharp rocks and sticks; pile 6 inches of dry insulation for a mattress.
Rig the simplest windproof cover: bag bivvy, lean-to, or tarp A-frame.
Change into anything dry; eat and drink if you can — calories are heat.
stop_conditions: Flash-flood terrain or rising water: move — no bivvy survives a torrent.
Lightning nearby: avoid ridges, lone trees, and metal — crouch low in a uniform stand of trees.

title: Plan a small vegetable garden layout
mechanism_check: Plants are solar panels — yield follows sunlight hours.
Tall plants shade short ones, so height steps down away from the sun side.
Paths are the real footprint: you work the paths, the beds just sit there.
improvised_tools: String and sticks to lay out beds full-size before digging.
A shadow stick or phone compass to map sun across the day.
steps: Watch the plot for a full day and map sun and shade.
Lay out beds no wider than you can reach across, about four feet.
Put tall crops on the north side so nothing gets shaded out.
Leave paths wide enough for a wheelbarrow; plant, mulch, water — and note what worked for next year.
stop_conditions: Under six hours of sun and you plant sun-lovers anyway: stop — pick shade crops or pick another plot.
No water within hose reach: stop — hand-carrying water fails within a week.

title: Build a compost bin from pallet wood
mechanism_check: Compost wants air, moisture, and mass — a bin is walls that hold a cubic yard while breathing.
Pallets are free slatted walls; the slats are the airflow.
Heat comes from volume: small piles stall, big piles cook.
improvised_tools: Heat-treated pallets (HT stamp) — never chemically treated ones.
Zip ties or wire for a no-tools build; a tarp for a lid.
steps: Pick four sound pallets; reject stained ones or any stamped MB.
Stand three as walls, wired solid at the corners.
Leave the front pallet loose or hinged for turning access.
Fill in layers — greens, browns, water — turn monthly, keep it damp as a wrung sponge.
stop_conditions: Pallets stamped MB (methyl bromide) or with chemical stains: stop — do not grow food in that.
Bin stays slimy and stinking: stop adding greens — it needs browns and air, not more food.
